label: Ventricular Rhythms (Lecture 13)
rows: ANY tachycardia that originates in the ventricles. 100–300 per minute, REGULAR (monomorphic), no P waves (or usually DISSOCIATED ones), no PR, WIDE QRS. With OR without a pulse.
IRREGULAR ventricular tachycardia, 100–300, complexes TWIST around the baseline ("twisting of the points"). ★ The form with a PROLONGED QT interval is called torsades de pointes.
Chaotic firing of MULTIPLE ventricular foci; the muscle QUIVERS. 300–500, irregular, NO measurable P, QRS or T. No contraction = NO cardiac output, NO pulse. Fine (small waves) or coarse.
Lack of electrical activity, no pulse: FLAT LINE. Untreated ventricular fibrillation ends here.
ORGANIZED electrical activity, NO palpable pulse (classically described as no mechanical activity). ★ Can look like ANY organized rhythm, even normal sinus; the missing PULSE makes the diagnosis.
Atria contract, ventricles do not: upright P waves MARCH across with NO QRS. No pulse, no cardiac output. Can be paroxysmal.

label: Telling the Ventricular Rhythms Apart
rows: ONE shape, regular vs CHANGING shape, irregular. Rate and width are shared and cannot separate them.
ORGANIZED identical complexes vs CHAOS with no measurable QRS. "You can see how organized V-tach truly is."
Small continuous waves vs a FLAT line.
Standstill keeps its P waves; asystole has none.

label: Paced Rhythms
rows: Spike → NORMAL P-QRS-T. Depends on an INTACT conduction pathway, so the QRS is narrow.
★ Spike married to EVERY QRS + WIDE QRS + CONTRALATERAL T wave (opposite to the QRS) = ventricle captured. Paces below the atria.
Dual-chamber pacemaker (common): a spike before the P wave AND before each wide QRS.

label: Atrioventricular Blocks
rows: A DELAY in, or complete FAILURE of, conduction of an atrial impulse through the atrioventricular node.
★ Sinus rhythm with PR BEYOND 0.2 s; ALL P waves conducted; BENIGN delay in the atrioventricular node. "The only thing you need to know … is the PR interval duration."
PR LENGTHENS until a P wave is not conducted, then resets: grouped beats. Irregular. In the atrioventricular NODE: conduction slows beat by beat until one impulse fails.

CONSTANT PR (normal or wide) with dropped QRS; ≥2 consecutive conducted beats before a drop; can drop >1 in a row. LESS common, MORE serious, ALMOST ALWAYS conduction disease. BELOW the node (His-Purkinje). QRS usually wide.
No P waves conducted: regular P-P UNRELATED to regular R-R, P waves march through the QRS-T. Atrial rate FASTER. Two pacemakers. QRS narrow or wide by escape origin.
Age-related FIBROSIS and acute myocardial infarction, especially INFERIOR.

label: Block Logic
rows: Find the dropped beat. Compare PR BEFORE vs AFTER it: DIFFERENT = type I (after is shorter); EQUAL = type II (except 2:1 block, where the two beats cannot tell you the type).
More P waves than QRS? → suggests a block. Then PR lengthening = type I, constant = type II, random = third-degree. (Long PR, nothing dropped = first-degree.)
Atrioventricular junction → NARROW QRS. Purkinje / bundle-branch fibers → WIDE QRS.
The ventricular impulse does not go back up to the atria, so the atria usually carry on alone and any P waves are usually dissociated.
